title: Client reactions, biases and the ethics of retention
objectives: Name the bias behind three common client statements.
Keep retention honest: no churning, no promises.
body_md:
## Common client reactions and responses

| Client says | Bias behind it | Respond with |
|---|---|---|
| "Let me stop my SIP until markets settle." | Loss aversion | "Your SIP is buying more units at lower prices now. Stopping skips the part that helps most later." |
| "My friend's fund gave 40%. Let's switch." | Recency / herd | "Let's compare both over 5 years and see how each did in bad years." |
| "I'll sell when it's back to my cost." | Anchoring | "Your buying price doesn't affect what the fund does next. Is it still the right fund for your goal?" |

## Ethics: what retention must never become

- No switching or churning that benefits commission rather than the client
- No pushing NFOs or new categories without a clear fit
- No assurance of returns, capital protection or recovery timelines

> **Investor takeaway:** A good distributor's value often shows up most when markets fall, by helping you stay invested.
example: A client says, 'My friend's fund gave 40%, let's switch.' You show both funds over 5 years, including bad years, and note the exit load and tax cost of switching.
say: Your buying price doesn't affect what the fund does next. Is it still the right fund for your goal?
Let's compare both funds over 5 years, including how each did in the bad years.
never: You're right, switch to the top performer.
Don't worry, it will definitely recover.

check.q: "I'll sell when it's back to my cost." Which bias is this?
check.why: The buying price doesn't affect what the fund does next. Ask if it's still the right fund for the goal.

check.q: "My friend's fund gave 40%. Let's switch." Which bias is this?
check.why: Respond by comparing both funds over 5 years, including how each did in bad years.

check.q: 'Let me stop my SIP until markets settle' mostly reflects which bias?
check.why: Loss aversion makes clients want to avoid further falls, even though SIPs benefit from lower prices.
